notes.text:
The cash ratios in this tool are built from the cash flow statement rather
than the income statement or balance sheet, which makes them harder to
distort with accounting choices — cash either moved or it didn't.

Free cash flow, FCF margin, and operating cash ratio together describe
whether a business generates enough actual cash to fund itself, cover its
near-term obligations, and have something left over. A company can be
profitable on paper (positive net income) while being cash-negative, and
this category is where that gap becomes visible.

The single most common way to misread these ratios is comparing a company
against a different-sector benchmark instead of its own peers.

A 25% gross margin is ordinary for a grocery chain and worrying for a
software company; a 2.0 debt-to-equity ratio is routine for a utility and
aggressive for a retailer. Every ratio in this tool is more informative
compared against the same company's own history, or against companies in
the same sector, than against a generic "good ratio" number that doesn't
account for what kind of business is being measured.

Grocery and restaurant chains collect cash from customers immediately but pay
suppliers on 30-60 day terms, so they can run current ratios below 1.0
indefinitely without distress. Walmart and Costco have both operated for
years with ratios near 0.8-0.9.

Software and SaaS companies tend to run the opposite way: minimal inventory
and large deferred-revenue cash balances produce current ratios of 3-5 that
don't indicate idle capital the way they would at an industrial company.

When this ratio reads unusually low or high, check the sector before
treating it as a signal either way.

The current ratio measures whether a company can cover its short-term
obligations with short-term assets.

Below 1.0 means current liabilities exceed current assets, which can signal
strain — though it is normal in businesses that collect cash before paying
suppliers, such as grocery and restaurant chains.

Between 1.5 and 3.0 is generally comfortable for most industries.

Above 3.0 is not automatically good. It can indicate capital sitting idle
rather than being deployed.

Software companies commonly run high current ratios because they carry no
inventory and hold large cash balances.

Capital-intensive and asset-backed businesses routinely run debt-to-equity
ratios well above what would be a warning sign elsewhere.

Utilities finance power plants and grids with long-term debt serviced by
predictable, regulated cash flows, and commonly carry ratios of 1.5-2.5 as a
matter of normal operation. Banks and other financial institutions are
structurally leveraged — deposits and borrowed funds are the business — and
conventional debt-to-equity thresholds don't apply to them at all (see the
banking sector note). REITs typically carry significant mortgage debt
against real estate holdings for similar reasons.

A ratio that looks alarming for a software company can be unremarkable for
a utility.

Debt to equity compares what a company owes to what its shareholders have
invested.

Below 0.5 is conservative — the balance sheet leans on equity financing,
which carries no fixed repayment obligation. 0.5-1.5 is a common, workable
range for most industries. Above 1.5 means liabilities substantially exceed
equity, which raises fixed obligations that must be met regardless of how
the business performs that year.

This ratio is undefined when equity is negative — dividing by a negative
number produces a mathematically valid but financially meaningless result,
so this tool withholds a number in that case rather than showing one that
would be misread as "very low debt."

Equity ratio and debt to equity describe the same balance sheet from two
angles and will usually agree, but they diverge in one important case:
negative equity.

Debt to equity becomes undefined and not meaningful when equity turns
negative, but equity ratio keeps working — a negative equity ratio is
exactly the signal that debt to equity can't show.

When you see a "not meaningful" debt-to-equity value, check the equity
ratio for the same year; it's often the more informative number in that
situation.

Equity ratio is the share of total assets financed by shareholders rather
than by creditors — total equity divided by total assets.

Below 25% means the balance sheet leans heavily on liabilities to fund what
the company owns. 25-50% is typical. Above 50% means shareholders, not
lenders, own most of the asset base — a structurally conservative position.

Unlike debt to equity, this ratio stays meaningful even when equity is
negative: a negative equity ratio is itself a legitimate (and serious) data
point, showing liabilities exceed total assets, rather than becoming
undefined the way debt-to-equity does.

Net margin and FCF margin measure different things and a gap between them
isn't a red flag by itself.

Depreciation and amortization reduce net income without using cash, so a
capital-intensive business can show FCF margin above net margin.
Conversely, a company investing heavily in growth capex can show healthy
net margin while FCF margin runs low or negative, because that spending
doesn't hit the income statement as an expense the way it hits the cash
flow statement as an outflow.

Look at the two together rather than expecting them to match.

FCF margin expresses free cash flow as a percentage of revenue, making it
comparable across companies of different sizes the way a raw free cash flow
dollar figure can't be.

Below 0% means the company burns cash relative to its revenue. 0-10% is a
common range for growing or capital-intensive businesses. Above 10%
indicates the business converts a meaningful share of every revenue dollar
into cash it can freely deploy.

Because it's built on cash flow rather than accounting net income, FCF
margin and net margin can diverge — a company can be net-income profitable
but cash-flow negative, or vice versa, depending on non-cash charges and
working-capital timing.

A single year of negative free cash flow is easy to misread as distress.

Capital-intensive businesses — telecoms building out networks, utilities
building generation capacity, retailers opening stores, any company
mid-expansion — go through years where capex spikes well above operating
cash flow by design.

The three-year trend matters more than any single year here: a company with
consistently negative free cash flow across multiple years, with no large
one-time capex program to point to, is a different and more concerning case
than one dip during an announced expansion.

Free cash flow is the cash a business generates from operations after
paying for the capital expenditures needed to maintain and grow it —
operating cash flow minus capex.

It's the cash actually available to pay down debt, return to shareholders,
or reinvest, and it's harder to distort with accounting choices than net
income, since it's built from cash movements rather than accruals.

Positive free cash flow means the business is self-funding. Negative free
cash flow isn't automatically a red flag — it's expected and often healthy
during a deliberate growth or capex cycle — but it does mean the company is
relying on existing cash, debt, or new equity to fund itself, which is
worth understanding.

Comparing gross margin across sectors is one of the most common
misreadings of this ratio.

Retail and grocery businesses typically run 20-35% because they resell
physical goods bought from suppliers at a markup. Manufacturers land in a
similar range once raw materials and labor are counted. Software, media, and
other businesses that sell a product with near-zero marginal cost to
reproduce routinely post 70-90%.

A 30% gross margin is unremarkable for a retailer and alarming for a
software company — the number only means something next to same-sector
peers.

Gross margin is revenue minus the direct cost of producing what was sold,
divided by revenue. It isolates pricing power and production efficiency
before overhead, R&D, and marketing enter the picture.

A grocery store might run a gross margin near 25%, a hardware retailer near
30-35%, and an enterprise software company north of 75% — none of those
numbers are "better" in isolation, they reflect fundamentally different cost
structures.

What matters more than the absolute level is whether it's stable or
expanding over time; a business that can raise prices or cut production
costs faster than its peers will show it here first.

A ratio's trend and its level are two different signals and shouldn't be
collapsed into one story.

A ratio can be improving while still weak — a company climbing out of a
difficult period — or declining while still strong — a company coming off
an unusually good year toward a more normal one. Both cases are common and
neither the trend nor the level alone tells the full story; the two
together are more informative than either in isolation.

Leverage ratios describe how a company's assets are financed — by
shareholders' equity or by borrowed money — and how much of a cushion
exists before creditors are affected by a downturn.

More leverage magnifies both gains and losses: it can boost returns to
equity holders in good years (see the ROE leverage-distortion note) and
accelerate distress in bad ones. There's no universally "correct" level of
leverage; the right amount depends heavily on how stable and predictable a
company's cash flows are, which is why the sector exception notes matter
more here than in almost any other category.

Liquidity ratios answer one question: can this company meet its
obligations that come due within roughly the next year, using assets that
are already cash or can become cash quickly?

They say nothing about long-term solvency, profitability, or growth — a
company can be highly liquid and still be shrinking, or tightly liquid and
still be a well-run, cash-up-front business (see the sector exception
notes). Liquidity ratios are best read as a floor check — is there a
near-term funding problem — rather than a measure of overall quality.

Total equity turns negative when a company's cumulative liabilities exceed
its cumulative assets — often the result of years of losses, large share
buybacks funded by debt, or leveraged transactions like spin-offs.

When equity is negative, return on equity and debt to equity become
mathematically computable but financially meaningless: dividing by a
negative number flips the sign in a way that makes a deeply troubled
company appear to have a suspiciously good-looking ratio. This tool
withholds a number for both ratios in that case and marks them "not
meaningful" rather than showing a misleading figure — the equity ratio,
which divides by total assets instead of equity, remains a meaningful (if
concerning) number in the same situation.

A single quarter or fiscal year of unusually high or low net margin is often
the result of a one-time event — an asset sale, a legal settlement, a
restructuring charge, a tax law change — rather than a change in the
underlying business.

Because this tool computes ratios from as-reported net income without
adjusting for one-off items, a sharp single-year spike or drop in net margin
is a prompt to look at what happened that year, not necessarily evidence the
business got better or worse.

Net margin is what's left of each dollar of revenue after every expense —
cost of goods, operating costs, interest, and taxes. It's the most complete
single-number profitability figure, but also the most exposed to one-off
items that have nothing to do with the ongoing business.

Below 0% means the company lost money over the period. 0-10% is common for
competitive, capital-intensive, or low-margin-by-design businesses (retail,
airlines, contractors). Above 10% suggests either strong pricing power or a
capital-light model.

Because it sits downstream of financing and tax decisions, net margin is
more useful compared against a company's own history than against a
different company's.

The current ratio and operating cash ratio can tell different stories in
the same year, and the gap is informative.

A company with a strong current ratio but a weak operating cash ratio may
be liquid on paper — sitting on receivables and inventory — while
struggling to convert operations into actual cash. That combination is
worth more attention than either ratio alone, since it's often an early
sign of collection problems or a slowing business before it shows up
elsewhere.

Operating cash ratio compares operating cash flow to current liabilities —
a stricter, harder-to-manipulate cousin of the current and quick ratios,
since it uses actual cash generated rather than assets that still need to
be converted to cash.

Below 0.5 means operating cash flow alone would cover less than half of
what's due in the short term. 0.5-1.0 is a reasonable working range. Above
1.0 means a company could cover its current liabilities from operating cash
flow alone, without touching existing cash reserves or selling assets.

Operating margin and net margin usually move together, but when they
diverge sharply it's worth asking why.

A company with a healthy operating margin but a much lower net margin is
typically carrying heavy interest expense from debt, a large one-time
charge, or an unusual tax situation — none of which reflect how the core
business is actually performing.

Conversely, a net margin propped up above operating margin (a one-time
gain, a tax credit) is not a repeatable result and shouldn't be read as an
improving trend.

Operating margin takes gross profit and subtracts the operating expenses
required to run the business day to day — R&D, sales, marketing,
administration — before interest and taxes. It answers a narrower question
than net margin: is the core business itself profitable, independent of how
it's financed or taxed.

Below 5% leaves little room for a downturn in demand or a cost spike. 5-15%
is typical for a mature, competitive business. Above 15% usually signals
real pricing power, scale advantages, or both.

A widening gap between gross margin and operating margin over time is worth
watching — it means operating costs are growing faster than the business.

Profitability ratios measure how much of each revenue dollar a company
keeps at different stages — after production costs, after operating costs,
after everything.

Read together rather than individually, the four profitability ratios in
this tool (gross, operating, and net margin, plus return on equity) show
where in the cost structure profit is being made or lost. A company with
strong gross margin but weak operating margin has a cost problem in
overhead or R&D, not in what it sells; a company with strong operating
margin but weak net margin has a financing or tax story, not an operating
one.

A wide gap between the current ratio and the quick ratio is itself
informative: it means a large share of current assets is tied up in
inventory.

That's expected and benign for a retailer around its inventory build-up
before a holiday season, but a growing gap over successive years can mean
inventory is piling up faster than it's selling — a working-capital problem
rather than a strength, even though the current ratio alone would look fine.

Read the two ratios together, not in isolation.

The quick ratio (also called the acid-test ratio) is the current ratio's
stricter sibling. It removes inventory from current assets before dividing
by current liabilities, because inventory is the current asset most likely
to take time, or a markdown, to convert to cash.

A quick ratio below 0.5 means a company would struggle to cover short-term
obligations without selling inventory or raising cash. 0.5-1.0 is workable
for most industries. Above 1.0 means liquid assets alone cover short-term
liabilities.

Because it strips out inventory, the quick ratio is usually more revealing
than the current ratio for manufacturers and retailers, and nearly identical
to the current ratio for companies that don't carry inventory at all.

Every ratio in this tool is computed from a company's financial statements —
what it owns, owes, earns, and spends — and none of them incorporate the
company's stock price, valuation multiples, or market sentiment.

A financially healthy company by these measures can be expensively or
cheaply priced by the market; these ratios say nothing about whether a
stock is a good purchase at its current price, because that question
depends on the price paid, not just the business's underlying financial
condition. This tool explains financial health, not investment value.

Return on equity measures how much profit a company generates for every
dollar shareholders have invested, net of what's owed to creditors.

Below 5% is weak — shareholders could often do better in a low-risk
alternative. 5-15% is a reasonable, sustainable range for most established
businesses. Above 15% is strong, though it deserves a second look (see the
note on leverage distortion) before assuming it reflects pure operating
efficiency.

ROE is undefined — not simply low — when a company has negative equity,
which is why this tool marks it not meaningful rather than showing a number
in that case.

Return on equity can be inflated by debt rather than genuine efficiency.

Because ROE divides by equity alone, a company that finances more of its
assets with borrowed money — shrinking the equity in the denominator — will
show a higher ROE even if its underlying profitability is unchanged. Two
companies with identical operating performance can post very different ROE
figures purely because one carries more debt.

Always read ROE alongside debt to equity: a high ROE paired with high
leverage is a different, riskier story than a high ROE paired with low
leverage.

A single fiscal year is a snapshot, and businesses with seasonal demand,
cyclical end markets, or lumpy large-contract revenue can look meaningfully
different depending on exactly when their fiscal year ends relative to
their business cycle. A retailer's fiscal year-end just after a strong
holiday quarter will show a different balance-sheet picture than one ending
mid-year.

This is part of why this tool shows a three-year trend rather than a single
year's ratios in isolation — but three years is still a short window for
businesses with longer cycles, and a single unusually strong or weak year
can still skew what "improving" or "declining" means.

Banks and other depository financial institutions report financial
statements in a fundamentally different shape than non-financial companies,
because their business is borrowing and lending money rather than buying
inventory and selling goods at a markup.

Concepts like "current assets," "current liabilities," "inventory," and
"capital expenditure" don't map cleanly onto a bank's balance sheet, so
several ratios in this tool — current ratio, quick ratio, gross margin,
operating margin, free cash flow, FCF margin, and operating cash ratio —
are typically unavailable for banks rather than computed from a forced
approximation. This is a coverage gap, not a data error.

Comparing a bank's available ratios (net margin, ROE, debt to equity,
equity ratio) against a non-financial company's is also not meaningful,
since a bank's leverage and margin structure are unlike any operating
company's by design.

Real estate investment trusts (REITs) carry structurally high leverage
because their business model is owning income-producing property financed
substantially with mortgage debt, and they're required to distribute most
of their taxable income as dividends rather than retaining it to pay down
debt or build equity organically.

Standard debt-to-equity and equity-ratio thresholds calibrated for
operating companies read as alarming applied to a REIT; sector-relative
comparison matters more here than almost anywhere else in this tool's
coverage.

Grocery and restaurant chains, and much of retail generally, are built
around a cash-conversion cycle where customers pay immediately (or on
delivery) while suppliers are paid on 30-90 day terms.

That structure lets a well-run retailer operate with a current ratio below
1.0 indefinitely — the company is effectively using supplier credit as
working capital rather than sitting on excess liquidity. Gross margins in
this sector are also lower by design (20-35% is typical) than in sectors
that don't resell physical goods bought at wholesale.

Software and SaaS companies have a cost structure unlike most other
businesses: minimal cost of goods sold (mostly cloud hosting), no physical
inventory, and revenue often collected as cash (subscriptions) ahead of
when it's recognized as earned.

This tends to produce very high gross margins (70-90%+), high current
ratios (large cash balances against modest current liabilities), and free
cash flow that's frequently stronger than net income, since stock-based
compensation and deferred revenue distort net income relative to actual
cash movement.

None of these are inflated or suspicious for this sector — they're
structural.

Utilities and other regulated, capital-intensive infrastructure businesses
finance long-lived physical assets (power plants, pipelines, grids) with
substantial long-term debt, supported by predictable, often regulated
revenue.

Debt-to-equity ratios of 1.5-2.5 that would be a warning sign at an
unregulated company are normal and expected here, because the cash flows
backing that debt are unusually stable. Growth in this sector is also
capital-expenditure heavy, so free cash flow is frequently low or negative
during active construction periods without indicating distress.

This tool's trend classification compares the earliest and latest of the
last three to four fiscal years of available data. That's enough to
separate a genuine multi-year direction from a single unusual year, but
it's still a short window for industries with longer cycles — commodities,
heavy industry, real estate development — where a full cycle can run five
to ten years.

A "stable" or "improving" trend over three years doesn't rule out a
longer-term cyclical pattern that a longer lookback would reveal.

Because free cash flow can swing year to year with the timing of a single
large capital project, a one-year decline is common and often unremarkable
(see the capex-cycle note).

A cash trend declining across three consecutive years, especially alongside
stable or growing revenue, is a more reliable signal that something
structural has changed — rising costs, slowing collections, or a business
that increasingly needs more capital to generate the same revenue.

A rising debt-to-equity trend isn't automatically bad — it often
accompanies a deliberate decision to fund growth, an acquisition, or a
share buyback with debt rather than diluting shareholders.

What matters is whether the increase is matched by the cash flow and
earnings to service it. A rising leverage trend paired with declining or
flat operating margin and free cash flow is a materially different
situation than the same rising leverage paired with strong and growing
cash generation.

A liquidity ratio declining over multiple years — even from a comfortable
starting point — is worth more attention than a single low reading.

It can mean current liabilities are growing faster than current assets,
which happens naturally during rapid growth (more payables, more
short-term debt to fund expansion) but can also signal that receivables or
inventory aren't converting to cash as fast as they used to. A single
year's dip during a known event (an acquisition, a large one-time payable)
is less concerning than a multi-year slide with no clear cause.

A profitability trend matters more than a profitability level, because it
captures direction: is the business getting more or less efficient at
turning revenue into profit.

A declining margin trend alongside flat or growing revenue often points to
rising input costs, pricing pressure from competitors, or a shift toward
lower-margin products or services. An improving trend alongside flat
revenue can indicate cost discipline or a favorable pricing shift. Margins
that stay flat for years in a competitive industry aren't a bad sign —
stability itself is a data point.

These ratios describe a company's financial position as reported in its
statements — they cannot tell you about the quality of its management, the
durability of its competitive position, pending litigation, regulatory
risk, or how its industry might change.

Two companies can post identical ratios across the board and face very
different futures for reasons no financial ratio captures. This tool is a
starting point for understanding financial health as reported, not a
complete picture of business quality or risk.
